title: The Secrets To Lessons Students Love
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that seven commonly recommended approaches to engaging lessons, entertaining, conceptual, vague, applicable, technological, superficial, and broad, are precisely what causes students to disengage, and that the real driver of compelling teaching is a teacher's depth of subject-matter expertise rather than any particular delivery method. He argues elementary-age students specifically are not ready for conceptual, big-picture learning until they have mastered basics through repetition, and that lessons obsessed with 'real-world applicability' actually bore students, who are instead drawn to unfamiliar, mysterious worlds (Edo Japan, Pasteur's lab, Roman battle-dress rituals) precisely because they have no prior connection to them. Linsin makes a sharper claim against classroom technology, arguing learning outcomes are worse across every measure compared to books, beakers, and math compasses, and that pencils and bound books develop fine motor skill and calm the mind in ways screens do not. His central diagnosis for why so many lessons fail is breadth: teacher guidebooks increasingly skim the surface of topics rather than going deep, a pattern he attributes both to politicians and publishers lowering the bar to match declining test scores, and to teachers not knowing their subject matter deeply enough to mine it for compelling detail. The piece closes by arguing students actively want to be challenged with content that is 'weird, scary, shocking, gross, sad, inspiring,' and that only a teacher with genuine subject-matter passion and depth can deliver that kind of engagement.
points: Linsin's central claim inverts common engagement advice: entertainment, technology, and real-world relevance are named as causes of disengagement, while a teacher's own depth of subject-matter expertise is identified as the actual driver of student interest.

He argues elementary-age students specifically are not developmentally ready for conceptual, big-picture learning until basics are mastered through repetition, directly challenging skills-first and inquiry-based instructional trends.

The claim that content students have 'little connection to' (Edo Japan, Roman battle-dress rituals) engages them more than manufactured real-world relevance (budgeting with 'imaginary money') reframes unfamiliarity as a pedagogical asset rather than a barrier.

His argument against classroom technology is stated in absolute terms, that learning outcomes are worse 'in every measure' compared to books and pencils, positioning handwriting and print as tools that develop fine motor skill and calm attention in ways screens cannot.

He identifies two specific structural causes for shallow lesson content: policy-driven lowering of the achievement bar in guidebooks, and teachers' own insufficient subject-matter depth, rather than attributing shallow teaching to time constraints alone.
quotes: If you try to entertain your students into paying attention with elaborate and ever-exciting activities, you will fail. You can't compete with their after-school, online world.
Repetition isn't a bad word. Rather, it's one of the most effective tools for learning and building confidence and self-worth.

It's the stuff they have little connection to, and have never heard of, that sparks their interest and desire to learn. Escaping into Edo Japan, Bastonge 1944, Pasteur's lab, Ramses reign, Black Widow Pulsars, and the 1000s of options you have to draw students into mysterious and fascinating worlds is what gets their heart racing.
Learning outcomes are worse in every measure compared to books, beakers, and math compasses. They already know more technology than most teachers. They already spend too much time staring at screens.
Teacher guidebooks and materials skim the surface of lesson topics, more now than ever before, which is equivalent to giving students Ambien-laced gummy bears.

Students want to be challenged. They want to be pushed. They want to learn something new, weird, scary, shocking, gross, sad, inspiring, amazing, and achingly beautiful. But it takes a teacher who knows their topic to deliver it.
